whats-new-at-sheridan.title: What's New at Sheridan
whats-new-at-sheridan.lede: What's New at Sheridan brings every campus event from the SSU, Sheridan Clubs, Sheridan EDGE and Sheridan College into one consistent, filterable calendar, so Sheridan students can find an event that matters to them in seconds instead of checking four separate websites.

facts.label: Built with
facts.value: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Node.js API, BeautifulSoup, Selenium, Claude, Vercel

highlights.label: organizer sites merged into one calendar
ways to narrow: date, campus, organizer, time of day
to add an event, or the whole week, to a calendar

sections.title: Events are spread across four websites

blocks.text: How might we reduce the effort it takes for Sheridan students to discover campus events that are relevant to them?

Sheridan students who want to get involved on campus have to check multiple sites to find out what's going on at the SSU, Sheridan Clubs, Sheridan EDGE and Sheridan College. Each one has a different layout and none of them shows the full picture, so finding events takes time and it's easy to miss the ones that would have mattered.

sections.title: One site for every campus event

blocks.text: We saw an opportunity to bring these sources together. The site pulls live event data from each organizer through an API we built by scraping their event pages, displays everything in one consistent format, and presents it in a single place. Students can narrow events by date, campus, organizer and time of day, see what's on this week at a glance, and add events straight to their calendar.

Before designing anything, we mapped where each organizer published events and what kind of events they ran. Every source lived on a different platform, with its own layout and its own way of describing dates, places and times. There was no shared structure to build on, so we had to define one.

Whatever the source, every event is normalized into the same set of fields. This shared model is what makes the site feel like one calendar rather than four feeds stitched together, and it is what the filters and layouts are built on.

blocks.text: Students don't look for events by data source. They ask when, where and who. Each question became a facet that can be combined with the others, so "What's on this evening at Trafalgar?" is two clicks away.

blocks.text: The page itself is ordered like an inverted pyramid. The most useful answer, how much is on this week, sits in the very first line, and each section below narrows from a broad overview to the specific event a student is looking for.

items.title: Navigation mirrors the facets
items.text: The main menu, This week · Organizers · Events · Campuses, maps directly to the ways students narrow events, so the menu doubles as a map of the content.

items.title: Every entry point lands on a filtered view
items.text: Choosing an organizer or campus anywhere on the page, including the footer, jumps to the event list with that filter already applied.

items.title: Plain, specific labels
items.text: "Evening (after 5 PM)" instead of a time code, and campus names paired with their city, so nobody has to guess what a label means.

items.title: Accessible by structure
items.text: A skip link straight to all events, colours checked against WCAG 2.2 AA, and event details that return focus where you left off.

blocks.text: Scrapers built with BeautifulSoup and Selenium collect events from each organizer's page, and a small API serves them in the shared format. The front end asks it for exactly the slice it needs, so every view and filter maps to a simple request.

items.title: Test with students on every campus
items.text: Watch how students from Davis, Trafalgar and HMC actually search, and refine the facets and labels around it.

items.title: Automate the scraping
items.text: Run the scrapers on a schedule so new events show up, and changed or cancelled ones update, without anyone having to refresh the data by hand.

items.title: Remember a student's filters
items.text: Let students keep their campus and favourite organizers so the page opens on what matters to them.

items.title: Bring in more organizers
items.text: The shared content model means a new source only needs a scraper, not a redesign.

retro-radio-speaker.title: Retro Radio + Speaker
retro-radio-speaker.lede: Retro Radio + Speaker is an illustrated infographic that labels the main parts of the PRUNUS J-150, a vintage-style radio packed with modern features, and walks new owners through using it in five simple steps, so a glamper can get music or a station playing at camp without opening a manual.

highlights.label: steps from switched off to listening
listening modes: Bluetooth, FM, AM and SW
ways to power it: solar, battery and DC 5V

preview.label: Infographic
preview.alt: Infographic titled Retro Radio + Speaker. A line drawing of the PRUNUS J-150 radio labels eleven parts: antenna, handle, phone stand, solar panel, battery entrance, Bluetooth controls, ports, tuning knob, mode switch, on-off knob and speaker. Below it, five illustrated steps show how to turn it on, connect Bluetooth, switch to radio, tune a station and extend the antenna.

blocks.text: The PRUNUS J-150 looks like an old-school transistor radio, with its wood-grain body and gold grille, but it hides modern features too: Bluetooth, a solar panel, a rechargeable battery, and USB and TF card playback. I chose it because I love how it mixes vintage style with new tech, and because there's a lot going on that isn't obvious at first glance.
Before drawing anything, I photographed the radio from every angle to find, understand and name each of its parts.

blocks.text: My research centred on a persona who goes glamping: camping, with a few comforts brought along. For someone setting up a radio at a campsite, the features that matter most are the ones that work away from a wall outlet, so the solar panel, battery, Bluetooth and antenna all earn a clear place on the diagram.
The five steps were tested with new users and iterated on based on where they got stuck, so the final instructions reflect how first-time owners actually use the radio.

The infographic answers the two questions a new owner has, in the order they ask them: what am I looking at, and how do I use it? The layout follows the path a reader's eye already takes, from the title at the top left, to the labelled diagram, to a row of steps read left to right.

touch-design-and-data.title: Touch: Design and Data
touch-design-and-data.lede: In April 2026, our team built an interactive floor installation that makes people feel as if they're swimming through water: as they move across the projection, bubble-like particles swirl around them to the sound of ocean waves crashing onto the shore. Using a Microsoft Kinect and TouchDesigner, it turns the body into the controller, creating a calm, instruction-free moment of escape that anyone can explore.

highlights.label: instructions or controllers: just step in and move
senses responding at once: sight and sound
every movement reflected in real time
research lenses: escapism, the butterfly effect and flow

preview.label: Video
preview.title: Touch: Design and Data, using the Microsoft Kinect and TouchDesigner

blocks.text: How might we create an immersive, interactive system where touch and movement shape sound and visuals in a way that users can feel, explore, and control using TouchDesigner and the Microsoft Kinect?

The idea started with touch, then grew into a whole responsive environment where the body itself is the interface. Instead of pressing buttons, people walk, reach and gesture, and the space answers back.

blocks.alt: A person walks across a floor projection of glowing blue and violet particles in a dim studio.
blocks.caption: Process work: experimenting with particle styles on the projected floor.

blocks.text: The idea was to make it feel as if you're swimming through water. The particles were designed to look like water bubbles, and the sound is an ocean wave crashing onto the shore. As people move, the bubbles swirl and part around them and the soundscape shifts with them. Pairing organic motion with calming sound creates a small digital piece of nature: a place to pause, breathe and play.

The whole experience is built around a single loop between the body, the visuals and the sound. There are no menus, modes or goals, so the structure stays simple enough to understand without being told: you move, the room responds, and you move again.

steps.name: You move
steps.note: Walk, reach or gesture anywhere on the floor

steps.name: The Kinect senses you
steps.note: Depth tracking picks out your body in the space

steps.name: TouchDesigner reads the motion
steps.note: Movement data is translated in real time

steps.name: The room responds
steps.note: Particles flow around you and the sound shifts

steps.name: You see it, hear it, move again

blocks.alt: Close-up of cyan particles on a dark floor, scattering around the shadows of hands and arms.
blocks.caption: Every movement leaves a ripple: particles part around hands and feet the moment they move.

items.title: No instructions needed
items.text: Nothing to read and nothing to learn. Simply walking in is enough to start.

items.title: Instant cause and effect
items.text: Every movement gets an immediate, visible and audible response, so people understand the system by using it.

items.title: Open to every body
items.text: Simple, full-body movement replaces precise control, so people of different abilities can take part.

items.title: Calm by design
items.text: Water-like motion and ambient sound keep the experience soothing rather than overwhelming.

blocks.text: People move through environments unconsciously, often unaware of how their actions affect the world around them. Our system makes that visible and immediate.

items.title: Escapism, done well
items.text: Structured, intentional escape can support emotional regulation and recovery rather than avoidance. Anup Bottu's TEDx talk on escapism vs. avoidance frames escape as a necessary cognitive break. Studies of simulated environments show responsive systems increase presence and agency, helping people feel grounded.

items.title: Our butterfly effect
items.text: Small actions can lead to larger, unpredictable outcomes. Research in embodied cognition shows we understand the world through physical interaction, so turning even subtle movements into visible ripples makes people more aware of their presence and its impact.

items.title: Flow theory
items.text: Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi's flow is a state of deep absorption fuelled by continuous, meaningful feedback. Immediate feedback, clear cause and effect and low cognitive load (Interaction Design Foundation) let people explore freely at their own pace.

blocks.text: The Kinect looks down on the floor and captures a depth image, where people show up as shapes against the ground. In TouchDesigner, that image is cleaned up to isolate bodies, then their movement is measured and used to push the particles and shape the sound, all in real time.

items.alt: A greyscale depth image in TouchDesigner showing two people from above as dark shapes on a light floor.
items.caption: The Kinect's depth view, thresholded so bodies stand out from the floor.

items.alt: A TouchDesigner node network on a monitor, with connected operators and a cloud of pink particles.
items.caption: The TouchDesigner network that turns that movement into particles and sound.

blocks.text: We broke the system into smaller parts and tested movement, visuals and sound separately to understand how each behaved. Through iterative testing, we refined how movement data controlled the particles and audio until the interaction felt responsive, intuitive and fluid.

items.title: The challenge
items.text: Learning Kinect body tracking and translating that data into meaningful interaction, aligning the projection in the physical space, and keeping the system responsive across multiple inputs.

items.title: How I worked through it
items.text: Breaking the system down, testing each part on its own, iterating constantly, troubleshooting with teammates, and reaching out for help with TouchDesigner when I needed it.

blocks.text: This project made me more confident working between physical and digital systems, and pushed me to think beyond functionality to how an environment can shape emotion, awareness and engagement. It reinforced the value of patience, iteration and adaptability, and showed me how challenges can lead to a more refined and meaningful experience.
If expanded further, the system could be developed into a space that more intentionally helps people enter a flow state, deepening their sense of calm, awareness and immersion.
